Part 1: Data Exploration & Preprocessing (8 points)¶

In this section, we will:

  1. Load the CIFAR-10 dataset and check its shape
  2. Split data into train, validation, and test sets (with class balance)
  3. Visualize sample images from each class
  4. Analyze class distribution to check balance
  5. Study pixel intensity and apply normalization
  6. Build a data augmentation pipeline (flips, rotations, zoom, contrast)
  7. Create an efficient tf.data pipeline with batching and prefetching

# Build data augmentation pipeline
data_augmentation = keras.Sequential([
    layers.RandomFlip("horizontal"),           # flip left-right
    layers.RandomRotation(0.1),                # rotate up to 10%
    layers.RandomZoom(0.1),                    # zoom in/out 10%
    layers.RandomContrast(0.1),                # change contrast
    layers.RandomTranslation(0.1, 0.1),        # shift up/down/left/right
], name="data_augmentation")

# Visualize augmentation on one sample image
sample_image = X_train_norm[0]  # take first image
sample_image_batch = np.expand_dims(sample_image, axis=0)  # add batch dim

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.subplot(2, 5, 1)
plt.imshow(sample_image)
plt.title("Original")
plt.axis('off')

# Show 9 augmented versions
for i in range(9):
    augmented = data_augmentation(sample_image_batch, training=True)
    plt.subplot(2, 5, i + 2)
    plt.imshow(augmented[0].numpy())
    plt.title(f"Augmented #{i+1}")
    plt.axis('off')

plt.suptitle(f"Data Augmentation on '{class_names[y_train[0]]}'", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("✅ Augmentation pipeline ready with: flip, rotation, zoom, contrast, translation")

In [9]:
# Build efficient tf.data pipelines
BATCH_SIZE = 64
AUTOTUNE = tf.data.AUTOTUNE

# Training dataset: shuffle + augment + batch + prefetch
train_ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_train_norm, y_train))
train_ds = train_ds.shuffle(buffer_size=1000, seed=SEED)
train_ds = train_ds.batch(BATCH_SIZE)
train_ds = train_ds.map(lambda x, y: (data_augmentation(x, training=True), y),
                        num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE)
train_ds = train_ds.prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

# Validation dataset: just batch + prefetch (no augmentation)
val_ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_val_norm, y_val))
val_ds = val_ds.batch(BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

# Test dataset: same as validation
test_ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_test_norm, y_test))
test_ds = test_ds.batch(BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

print("✅ Data pipelines ready:")
print(f"  Train batches:      {len(list(train_ds))}")
print(f"  Validation batches: {len(list(val_ds))}")
print(f"  Test batches:       {len(list(test_ds))}")
print(f"  Batch size:         {BATCH_SIZE}")

# Verify one batch shape
for batch_images, batch_labels in train_ds.take(1):
    print(f"\nBatch image shape: {batch_images.shape}")
    print(f"Batch label shape: {batch_labels.shape}")

Part 1 Summary¶

What we did:

  • Loaded CIFAR-10: 45,000 training + 5,000 validation + 10,000 test images
  • Data is perfectly balanced across all 10 classes (4,500 images per class in train)
  • Normalized pixel values from [0, 255] to [0, 1] for stable training
  • Built a rich augmentation pipeline: horizontal flip, rotation, zoom, contrast, translation
  • Created efficient tf.data pipelines with batching, shuffling, and prefetching

Why these choices:

  • Stratified split keeps class balance in validation set (important for fair evaluation)
  • Normalization to [0,1] helps gradient descent converge faster
  • Augmentation adds ~5× more visual variety without needing more data, reducing overfitting
  • Prefetch + parallel calls keep the GPU busy (no waiting for CPU to prepare data)

Part 2: Custom CNN Architecture Design (12 points)¶

In this section, we will design and train 3 custom CNN models with increasing complexity:

  1. Model A — Baseline CNN: simple convolutional blocks with pooling
  2. Model B — Improved CNN: adds Batch Normalization and Dropout for regularization
  3. Model C — Residual CNN: uses skip connections (ResNet-style blocks)

After training, we will compare:

  • Training accuracy vs validation accuracy
  • Test accuracy
  • Number of parameters
  • Training time

We also explore different kernel sizes, pooling strategies, and activation functions.

In [10]:
# Helper function to plot training history
def plot_history(history, title="Training History"):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

    # Accuracy plot
    axes[0].plot(history.history['accuracy'], label='Train', linewidth=2)
    axes[0].plot(history.history['val_accuracy'], label='Validation', linewidth=2)
    axes[0].set_title(f'{title} - Accuracy')
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Epoch')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('Accuracy')
    axes[0].legend()
    axes[0].grid(True)

    # Loss plot
    axes[1].plot(history.history['loss'], label='Train', linewidth=2)
    axes[1].plot(history.history['val_loss'], label='Validation', linewidth=2)
    axes[1].set_title(f'{title} - Loss')
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Epoch')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Loss')
    axes[1].legend()
    axes[1].grid(True)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


# Helper function to train a model and track time
def train_model(model, train_ds, val_ds, epochs=15, model_name="model"):
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Training: {model_name}")
    print(f"{'='*60}")

    # Early stopping: stop if val_loss doesn't improve for 5 epochs
    early_stop = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
        monitor='val_loss',
        patience=5,
        restore_best_weights=True,
        verbose=1
    )

    start_time = time.time()
    history = model.fit(
        train_ds,
        validation_data=val_ds,
        epochs=epochs,
        callbacks=[early_stop],
        verbose=1
    )
    train_time = time.time() - start_time

    print(f"\n⏱️ Training time: {train_time:.1f} seconds")
    return history, train_time


# Helper function to evaluate on test set
def evaluate_model(model, test_ds, model_name="model"):
    test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(test_ds, verbose=0)
    print(f"✅ {model_name} Test Accuracy: {test_acc*100:.2f}% | Test Loss: {test_loss:.4f}")
    return test_acc, test_loss

Model A: Baseline CNN¶

A simple CNN with 3 convolutional blocks. Each block: Conv2D → MaxPooling2D. No Batch Normalization, no Dropout. This is our starting point to beat.

In [11]:
def build_baseline_cnn(input_shape=(32, 32, 3), num_classes=10):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=input_shape)

    # Block 1
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same')(inputs)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2))(x)

    # Block 2
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2))(x)

    # Block 3
    x = layers.Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2))(x)

    # Classifier head
    x = layers.Flatten()(x)
    x = layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(x)

    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="baseline_cnn")


# Build, compile, and train
model_a = build_baseline_cnn()
model_a.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)
model_a.summary()

history_a, time_a = train_model(model_a, train_ds, val_ds, epochs=15,
                                model_name="Model A - Baseline CNN")
plot_history(history_a, "Model A: Baseline CNN")
test_acc_a, test_loss_a = evaluate_model(model_a, test_ds, "Model A - Baseline CNN")

Model B: Improved CNN with BatchNorm + Dropout¶

Same structure as Model A, but we add:

  • Batch Normalization after each Conv layer → faster, more stable training
  • Dropout in the classifier → reduces overfitting
  • Two Conv layers per block → deeper feature extraction
In [12]:
def build_improved_cnn(input_shape=(32, 32, 3), num_classes=10):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=input_shape)

    # Block 1
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), padding='same')(inputs)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2))(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.2)(x)

    # Block 2
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2))(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)

    # Block 3
    x = layers.Conv2D(128, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(128, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2))(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.4)(x)

    # Classifier head
    x = layers.Flatten()(x)
    x = layers.Dense(256, activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(x)

    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="improved_cnn")


# Build, compile, and train
model_b = build_improved_cnn()
model_b.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)
model_b.summary()

history_b, time_b = train_model(model_b, train_ds, val_ds, epochs=25,
                                model_name="Model B - Improved CNN")
plot_history(history_b, "Model B: Improved CNN")
test_acc_b, test_loss_b = evaluate_model(model_b, test_ds, "Model B - Improved CNN")

Model C: Residual CNN (ResNet-style)¶

This model uses skip connections. The key idea: the output of a block is block(x) + x. This helps gradients flow backward in deep networks, avoiding the "vanishing gradient" problem. This is the core idea behind ResNet, one of the most successful CNN architectures.

In [13]:
def residual_block(x, filters, stride=1):
    """A single residual block with skip connection."""
    shortcut = x

    # Main path
    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, (3, 3), strides=stride, padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)

    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)

    # If shape changed (stride > 1 or different filters), project the shortcut
    if stride != 1 or shortcut.shape[-1] != filters:
        shortcut = layers.Conv2D(filters, (1, 1), strides=stride, padding='same')(shortcut)
        shortcut = layers.BatchNormalization()(shortcut)

    # Add skip connection
    x = layers.Add()([x, shortcut])
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    return x


def build_residual_cnn(input_shape=(32, 32, 3), num_classes=10):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=input_shape)

    # Initial conv
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), padding='same')(inputs)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)

    # Stage 1: two residual blocks with 32 filters
    x = residual_block(x, 32)
    x = residual_block(x, 32)

    # Stage 2: two residual blocks with 64 filters (downsample)
    x = residual_block(x, 64, stride=2)
    x = residual_block(x, 64)

    # Stage 3: two residual blocks with 128 filters (downsample)
    x = residual_block(x, 128, stride=2)
    x = residual_block(x, 128)

    # Classifier head
    x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.4)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(x)

    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="residual_cnn")


# Build, compile, and train
model_c = build_residual_cnn()
model_c.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)
model_c.summary()

history_c, time_c = train_model(model_c, train_ds, val_ds, epochs=25,
                                model_name="Model C - Residual CNN")
plot_history(history_c, "Model C: Residual CNN")
test_acc_c, test_loss_c = evaluate_model(model_c, test_ds, "Model C - Residual CNN")

Part 2 Summary¶

Actual results:

Model Parameters Test Accuracy Notes
A: Baseline 357K 71.24% Simple 3-block CNN, no regularization
B: Improved (BN+Dropout) 817K 75.89% Underfit slightly — could use more epochs
C: Residual (ResNet-style) 700K 79.47% 🏆 Best custom model

Key findings:

  • Model A (Baseline): Overfits quickly (train acc > val acc). A simple CNN is a reasonable starting point but lacks modern tricks.
  • Model B (BatchNorm + Dropout): Added regularization reduced overfitting, but the model didn't fully converge in 25 epochs — training accuracy was only 75.6% suggesting room to grow.
  • Model C (Residual): Best performance with fewer parameters than Model B thanks to Global Average Pooling replacing Flatten. Skip connections helped deeper training without vanishing gradients.

Best custom model: Model C (Residual CNN) at 79.47% test accuracy.

Lesson learned: Architectural choices (residual connections, global average pooling) matter more than just "adding more layers". However, even our best custom model is outperformed by transfer learning (Part 3) — modern practice favors starting with pretrained weights when possible.

Part 3: Transfer Learning Implementation (15 points)¶

In this section, we use 3 pre-trained models from ImageNet and adapt them to CIFAR-10:

  1. VGG16 — classic, deep network with small 3×3 filters
  2. ResNet50 — uses residual connections, very deep (50 layers)
  3. EfficientNetB0 — modern, compound-scaled architecture

For each model, we try two strategies:

  • Feature Extraction: freeze the pre-trained layers, only train a new classifier head
  • Fine-tuning: unfreeze the top few layers and train with a very small learning rate

Why resize images? CIFAR-10 is 32×32 but these pre-trained models expect 96×96 or bigger. We use a Resizing layer to upscale before feeding into the base model.

Why small learning rate for fine-tuning? Pre-trained weights are already good. We just want to nudge them — not destroy them.

In [19]:
# Pre-trained models need bigger images
TL_IMAGE_SIZE = 96
TL_BATCH_SIZE = 64

# Build separate data pipelines WITHOUT pre-normalizing
# (each pre-trained model has its own preprocessing function)
train_ds_tl = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_train.astype('float32'), y_train))
train_ds_tl = train_ds_tl.shuffle(1000, seed=SEED).batch(TL_BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

val_ds_tl = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_val.astype('float32'), y_val))
val_ds_tl = val_ds_tl.batch(TL_BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

test_ds_tl = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_test.astype('float32'), y_test))
test_ds_tl = test_ds_tl.batch(TL_BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

print(f"✅ Transfer learning pipelines ready")
print(f"   Image size for pre-trained models: {TL_IMAGE_SIZE}x{TL_IMAGE_SIZE}")
print(f"   Batch size: {TL_BATCH_SIZE}")


# Build a FRESH augmentation pipeline for transfer learning
# (without fixed input shape — so it works on any size)
tl_augmentation = keras.Sequential([
    layers.RandomFlip("horizontal"),
    layers.RandomRotation(0.1),
    layers.RandomZoom(0.1),
    layers.RandomContrast(0.1),
], name="tl_augmentation")


# Generic function to build a transfer learning model
def build_tl_model(base_model_class, preprocess_fn, base_name,
                   image_size=TL_IMAGE_SIZE, num_classes=10,
                   trainable_base=False, unfreeze_last_n=0):
    """
    Build a transfer learning model.
    - base_model_class: the Keras application (e.g., keras.applications.VGG16)
    - preprocess_fn: the matching preprocess_input function
    - trainable_base: if True, fine-tuning mode; if False, feature extraction mode
    - unfreeze_last_n: number of top layers to unfreeze (only used if trainable_base=True)
    """
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))

    # Apply augmentation on 32x32 images FIRST (before resizing)
    x = tl_augmentation(inputs)

    # Resize to match pre-trained input size
    x = layers.Resizing(image_size, image_size)(x)

    # Apply model-specific preprocessing (scales pixels the way the base expects)
    x = layers.Lambda(preprocess_fn)(x)

    # Load pre-trained base (without top classifier)
    base_model = base_model_class(
        include_top=False,
        weights='imagenet',
        input_shape=(image_size, image_size, 3)
    )

    # Freeze everything first
    base_model.trainable = False

    # If fine-tuning, unfreeze last N layers
    if trainable_base and unfreeze_last_n > 0:
        base_model.trainable = True
        for layer in base_model.layers[:-unfreeze_last_n]:
            layer.trainable = False

    x = base_model(x, training=False)
    x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)
    x = layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(x)

    model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name=f"tl_{base_name}")
    return model, base_model


# Storage for results
tl_results = []

✅ Transfer learning pipelines ready
   Image size for pre-trained models: 96x96
   Batch size: 64

Experiment 1: VGG16 — Feature Extraction¶

Freeze all VGG16 layers. Only train the classifier head on top. This treats VGG16 as a fixed feature extractor.

In [20]:
model_vgg_fe, base_vgg = build_tl_model(
    base_model_class=keras.applications.VGG16,
    preprocess_fn=keras.applications.vgg16.preprocess_input,
    base_name="vgg16_feature_extract",
    trainable_base=False
)

model_vgg_fe.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

print(f"VGG16 Feature Extraction — Total params: {model_vgg_fe.count_params():,}")

history_vgg_fe, time_vgg_fe = train_model(
    model_vgg_fe, train_ds_tl, val_ds_tl, epochs=10,

)
test_acc_vgg_fe, _ = evaluate_model(model_vgg_fe, test_ds_tl, "VGG16 Feature Extraction")

Experiment 2: VGG16 — Fine-Tuning¶

Unfreeze the last 4 layers of VGG16 and train with a very small learning rate (1e-5). This lets the top layers adapt slightly to CIFAR-10 while keeping early layers stable.

In [21]:
model_vgg_ft, _ = build_tl_model(
    base_model_class=keras.applications.VGG16,
    preprocess_fn=keras.applications.vgg16.preprocess_input,
    base_name="vgg16_finetune",
    trainable_base=True,
    unfreeze_last_n=4
)

model_vgg_ft.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-5),  # Much smaller!
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

print(f"VGG16 Fine-Tuning — Trainable params: {sum([tf.size(v).numpy() for v in model_vgg_ft.trainable_variables]):,}")

history_vgg_ft, time_vgg_ft = train_model(
    model_vgg_ft, train_ds_tl, val_ds_tl, epochs=10,
    model_name="VGG16 Fine-Tuning"
)
test_acc_vgg_ft, _ = evaluate_model(model_vgg_ft, test_ds_tl, "VGG16 Fine-Tuning")

tl_results.append({
    'Model': 'VGG16',
    'Strategy': 'Fine-Tuning',
    'Test Accuracy': test_acc_vgg_ft,
    'Training Time (s)': time_vgg_ft,
    'Parameters': model_vgg_ft.count_params()
})
plot_history(history_vgg_ft, "VGG16 Fine-Tuning")

Experiment 3: ResNet50 — Feature Extraction¶

ResNet50 is deeper than VGG16 but has fewer parameters because it uses bottleneck blocks and residual connections.

Experiment 5: EfficientNetB0 — Feature Extraction¶

EfficientNetB0 is the newest of the three. It balances depth, width, and resolution using "compound scaling". It has fewer parameters than VGG or ResNet but often gets higher accuracy.

In [24]:

    preprocess_fn=keras.applications.efficientnet.preprocess_input,

    trainable_base=False
)

Part 3 Summary¶

Results (test accuracy):

Model Feature Extraction Fine-Tuning Winner
VGG16 80.31% 87.63% Fine-tune (+7.3%)
ResNet50 85.32% 88.00% 🏆 Fine-tune (+2.7%)
EfficientNetB0 85.23% 84.28% ⚠️ FE wins!

Key findings:

  1. ResNet50 Fine-Tuned is the best overall model at 88.00% test accuracy — this is our champion model.

  2. Fine-tuning usually beats feature extraction — but there's an important exception:

  3. EfficientNetB0 anomaly: Fine-tuning actually hurt EfficientNet (-1%). This is a well-known issue with EfficientNet and happens because:

    • EfficientNet relies heavily on BatchNorm statistics learned during ImageNet pretraining
    • When we unfreeze BN layers with a small CIFAR-10 batch, the running statistics drift
    • This "breaks" the pre-trained features that were working well
    • Fix: freeze BN layers during fine-tuning, or use larger batch sizes
    • For this case study, we accept this finding as a valid experimental result

  4. VGG16 benefits most from fine-tuning (+7.3%) because its features are older/less general than ResNet/EfficientNet. Updating them helps a lot on a new domain.

  5. Parameter efficiency: EfficientNetB0 has only 4.21M params — 5× smaller than ResNet50 and 3.5× smaller than VGG16 — yet reaches comparable accuracy. Modern architectures are fundamentally more efficient.

  6. Learning rate matters a lot for fine-tuning — we used 1e-5 (100× smaller than feature extraction's 1e-3). Using 1e-3 during fine-tuning would destroy the pre-trained weights.

Compute vs Accuracy Trade-off:

  • For speed: EfficientNetB0 Feature Extraction (269s, 85.23%)
  • For accuracy: ResNet50 Fine-Tuning (598s, 88.00%) 🏆
  • For memory-constrained: EfficientNetB0 wins by far (4.21M params)

Comparison to Custom CNN (Part 2): Our best custom model (Model C Residual, 79.47%) is clearly beaten by transfer learning. ResNet50 Fine-Tuned at 88% is +8.5% higher — a huge gap. This is the power of ImageNet pretraining: features learned from 1.2M diverse images transfer well to CIFAR-10 with minimal adaptation.

Part 4: Advanced CNN Techniques (6 points)¶

In this section, we explore modern techniques used in state-of-the-art CNNs:

  1. Squeeze-and-Excitation (Channel Attention) — lets the network focus on important feature channels
  2. Spatial Attention — lets the network focus on important spatial regions
  3. Label Smoothing — prevents overconfidence in predictions
  4. Learning Rate Scheduling — Cosine Decay for smoother convergence
  5. Grad-CAM Visualization — shows what the CNN "looks at" when making predictions
  6. Filter Visualization — shows what patterns early layers learn

We build on the Residual CNN (Model C) from Part 2 as our base.

4.1 — Squeeze-and-Excitation Block (Channel Attention)¶

The SE Block re-weights each feature channel based on its importance:

  1. Squeeze: Global average pool each channel into a single number
  2. Excitation: Two Dense layers learn a weight (0 to 1) per channel
  3. Scale: Multiply original features by these weights

This tells the network "which channels matter most" for the current image.

In [27]:
def se_block(x, reduction=16):
    """Squeeze-and-Excitation block for channel attention."""
    channels = x.shape[-1]

    # Squeeze: global average pool
    se = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    se = layers.Reshape((1, 1, channels))(se)

    # Excitation: two Dense layers
    se = layers.Dense(channels // reduction, activation='relu')(se)
    se = layers.Dense(channels, activation='sigmoid')(se)

    # Scale: multiply with input
    return layers.Multiply()([x, se])


def residual_block_with_se(x, filters, stride=1):
    """Residual block enhanced with SE attention."""
    shortcut = x

    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, (3, 3), strides=stride, padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)

    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)

    # Add SE attention
    x = se_block(x)

    if stride != 1 or shortcut.shape[-1] != filters:
        shortcut = layers.Conv2D(filters, (1, 1), strides=stride, padding='same')(shortcut)
        shortcut = layers.BatchNormalization()(shortcut)

    x = layers.Add()([x, shortcut])
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    return x


def build_se_resnet(input_shape=(32, 32, 3), num_classes=10):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=input_shape)
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), padding='same')(inputs)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)

    x = residual_block_with_se(x, 32)
    x = residual_block_with_se(x, 32)

    x = residual_block_with_se(x, 64, stride=2)
    x = residual_block_with_se(x, 64)

    x = residual_block_with_se(x, 128, stride=2)
    x = residual_block_with_se(x, 128)

    x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.4)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="se_resnet")


# Build, compile, and train
model_se = build_se_resnet()
model_se.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)
print(f"SE-ResNet parameters: {model_se.count_params():,}")

history_se, time_se = train_model(model_se, train_ds, val_ds, epochs=20,
                                  model_name="SE-ResNet (Channel Attention)")
test_acc_se, _ = evaluate_model(model_se, test_ds, "SE-ResNet")
plot_history(history_se, "SE-ResNet (Channel Attention)")

4.2 — Spatial Attention¶

While channel attention asks "which channel matters", spatial attention asks "which location matters". We compute a single attention map over the image using average + max pooling across channels.

In [29]:
def spatial_attention(x):
    """Spatial attention block — uses keras.ops for Keras 3 compatibility."""
    # Pool across channel dimension using keras.ops (not tf.reduce_*)
    avg_pool = layers.Lambda(lambda t: keras.ops.mean(t, axis=-1, keepdims=True))(x)
    max_pool = layers.Lambda(lambda t: keras.ops.max(t, axis=-1, keepdims=True))(x)

    # Concatenate and apply 7x7 conv
    concat = layers.Concatenate(axis=-1)([avg_pool, max_pool])
    attention = layers.Conv2D(1, (7, 7), padding='same', activation='sigmoid')(concat)

    return layers.Multiply()([x, attention])


def residual_block_with_spatial(x, filters, stride=1):
    shortcut = x

    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, (3, 3), strides=stride, padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)

    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, (3, 3), padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)

    x = spatial_attention(x)

    if stride != 1 or shortcut.shape[-1] != filters:
        shortcut = layers.Conv2D(filters, (1, 1), strides=stride, padding='same')(shortcut)
        shortcut = layers.BatchNormalization()(shortcut)

    x = layers.Add()([x, shortcut])
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)
    return x


def build_spatial_resnet(input_shape=(32, 32, 3), num_classes=10):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=input_shape)
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), padding='same')(inputs)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.ReLU()(x)

    x = residual_block_with_spatial(x, 32)
    x = residual_block_with_spatial(x, 32)
    x = residual_block_with_spatial(x, 64, stride=2)
    x = residual_block_with_spatial(x, 64)
    x = residual_block_with_spatial(x, 128, stride=2)
    x = residual_block_with_spatial(x, 128)

    x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.4)(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation='softmax')(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="spatial_resnet")


model_sp = build_spatial_resnet()
model_sp.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-3),
    loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)
print(f"Spatial Attention ResNet parameters: {model_sp.count_params():,}")

history_sp, time_sp = train_model(model_sp, train_ds, val_ds, epochs=20,
                                  model_name="Spatial Attention ResNet")
test_acc_sp, _ = evaluate_model(model_sp, test_ds, "Spatial Attention ResNet")

4.3 — Label Smoothing + Cosine Learning Rate Schedule¶

Two techniques combined:

  • Label Smoothing (0.1): instead of [0,0,1,0,...], target becomes [0.01, 0.01, 0.91, 0.01, ...]. This prevents the model from being overconfident and improves generalization.
  • Cosine Decay LR: Learning rate smoothly decreases following a cosine curve, typically giving better final accuracy than step decay.

Note: Label smoothing requires CategoricalCrossentropy (one-hot labels), so we convert labels.

In [30]:
# Convert labels to one-hot for label smoothing
y_train_oh = keras.utils.to_categorical(y_train, 10)
y_val_oh = keras.utils.to_categorical(y_val, 10)
y_test_oh = keras.utils.to_categorical(y_test, 10)

# One-hot datasets
train_ds_oh = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_train_norm, y_train_oh))
train_ds_oh = train_ds_oh.shuffle(1000, seed=SEED).batch(BATCH_SIZE)
train_ds_oh = train_ds_oh.map(lambda x, y: (data_augmentation(x, training=True), y),
                              num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

val_ds_oh = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_val_norm, y_val_oh))
val_ds_oh = val_ds_oh.batch(BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

test_ds_oh = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_test_norm, y_test_oh))
test_ds_oh = test_ds_oh.batch(BATCH_SIZE).prefetch(AUTOTUNE)

# Build fresh SE-ResNet for this experiment
model_ls = build_se_resnet()

# Cosine decay LR schedule
steps_per_epoch = len(X_train) // BATCH_SIZE
lr_schedule = keras.optimizers.schedules.CosineDecay(
    initial_learning_rate=1e-3,
    decay_steps=steps_per_epoch * 20
)

# Compile with label smoothing
model_ls.compile(
    optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=lr_schedule),
    loss=keras.losses.CategoricalCrossentropy(label_smoothing=0.1),
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

history_ls, time_ls = train_model(model_ls, train_ds_oh, val_ds_oh, epochs=20,
                                  model_name="SE-ResNet + Label Smoothing + Cosine LR")
test_loss_ls, test_acc_ls = model_ls.evaluate(test_ds_oh, verbose=0)
print(f"✅ SE-ResNet + LS + Cosine — Test Accuracy: {test_acc_ls*100:.2f}%")
plot_history(history_ls, "Label Smoothing + Cosine LR")

4.4 — Optimizer Comparison¶

We compare three popular optimizers on the same architecture:

  • Adam: adaptive momentum, works well out-of-the-box
  • SGD with momentum: traditional, often generalizes better with good tuning
  • AdamW: Adam with proper weight decay, often best for large models

⚠️ Note on optimizer comparison: Each optimizer was trained for only 10 epochs (to save time), which is insufficient for convergence on Model B's architecture (~800K parameters). The same architecture reached 75.89% with 25 epochs (see Part 2). So the absolute values here (62-69%) are below potential. The relative ranking is indicative:

  • Adam converges fastest in the first 10 epochs
  • SGD+Momentum often catches up and surpasses Adam with more epochs
  • AdamW benefits from longer schedules where weight decay kicks in

Treat this comparison as "early training behavior" not "final convergence".

4.5 — Grad-CAM Visualization (Model Interpretability)¶

Grad-CAM shows which parts of the image the CNN focuses on when making a prediction. It works by:

  1. Taking the last convolutional layer's feature maps
  2. Computing gradients of the predicted class with respect to these maps
  3. Weighting feature maps by these gradients
  4. Creating a heatmap overlaid on the original image

This is required for Part 5 analysis.

In [35]:
def get_last_conv_layer_name(model):
    """Find the name of the last Conv2D layer."""
    for layer in reversed(model.layers):
        if isinstance(layer, layers.Conv2D):
            return layer.name
    raise ValueError("No Conv2D layer found")


def make_gradcam_heatmap(img_array, model, last_conv_layer_name, pred_index=None):
    """Generate Grad-CAM heatmap."""
    # Build grad_model using functional API (fixes Keras 3 warning)
    grad_model = keras.Model(
        inputs=model.input,
        outputs=[model.get_layer(last_conv_layer_name).output, model.output]
    )

    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        conv_outputs, predictions = grad_model(img_array, training=False)
        if pred_index is None:
            pred_index = tf.argmax(predictions[0])
        class_channel = predictions[:, pred_index]

    grads = tape.gradient(class_channel, conv_outputs)
    pooled_grads = tf.reduce_mean(grads, axis=(0, 1, 2))

    conv_outputs = conv_outputs[0]
    heatmap = conv_outputs @ pooled_grads[..., tf.newaxis]
    heatmap = tf.squeeze(heatmap)

    heatmap = tf.maximum(heatmap, 0) / (tf.math.reduce_max(heatmap) + 1e-8)
    return heatmap.numpy()


def display_gradcam(img, heatmap, alpha=0.5):
    """Overlay heatmap on image."""
    heatmap_resized = cv2.resize(heatmap, (img.shape[1], img.shape[0]))
    heatmap_color = cv2.applyColorMap(np.uint8(255 * heatmap_resized), cv2.COLORMAP_JET)
    heatmap_color = cv2.cvtColor(heatmap_color, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB) / 255.0

    img_display = img if img.max() <= 1.0 else img / 255.0
    overlay = heatmap_color * alpha + img_display * (1 - alpha)
    return np.clip(overlay, 0, 1)


# Use Model C (Residual CNN) — simplest model for Grad-CAM since it has no nested base model.
# Its 79.47% accuracy is representative of what the network learned.
best_custom_model = model_c
last_conv_name = get_last_conv_layer_name(best_custom_model)
print(f"Using model: {best_custom_model.name}")
print(f"Last Conv layer: {last_conv_name}")

# Pick 6 random test images
np.random.seed(SEED)
sample_indices = np.random.choice(len(X_test_norm), 6, replace=False)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(18, 6))

for i, idx in enumerate(sample_indices):
    img = X_test_norm[idx]
    img_batch = np.expand_dims(img, axis=0).astype('float32')

    preds = best_custom_model.predict(img_batch, verbose=0)
    pred_class = np.argmax(preds[0])
    true_class = y_test[idx]

    heatmap = make_gradcam_heatmap(img_batch, best_custom_model, last_conv_name)
    overlay = display_gradcam(img, heatmap)

    axes[0, i].imshow(img)
    axes[0, i].set_title(f"True: {class_names[true_class]}\nPred: {class_names[pred_class]}",
                         fontsize=10,
                         color='green' if pred_class == true_class else 'red')
    axes[0, i].axis('off')

    axes[1, i].imshow(overlay)
    axes[1, i].set_title("Grad-CAM", fontsize=10)
    axes[1, i].axis('off')

plt.suptitle("Grad-CAM on Model C (Residual CNN): What the CNN Focuses On",
             fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4.6 — First Layer Filter Visualization¶

Visualizing the filters of the first Conv layer shows the basic patterns the CNN learned. Usually these are edges, colors, and simple textures — similar to what the human visual cortex detects.

# Get weights of the first Conv2D layer from our best custom model (Model C)
first_conv = None
for layer in best_custom_model.layers:
    if isinstance(layer, layers.Conv2D):
        first_conv = layer
        break

# Normalize filters to 0-1 for display
f_min, f_max = filters.min(), filters.max()
filters_norm = (filters - f_min) / (f_max - f_min + 1e-8)

n_filters = min(filters_norm.shape[-1], 32)
cols = 8
rows = int(np.ceil(n_filters / cols))

plt.figure(figsize=(cols * 1.5, rows * 1.5))
for i in range(n_filters):
    plt.subplot(rows, cols, i + 1)
    f = filters_norm[:, :, :, i]
    plt.imshow(f)
    plt.title(f"Filter {i+1}", fontsize=8)
    plt.axis('off')

weighted avg       0.88      0.88      0.88     10000

Part 4 Summary¶

Results of advanced techniques (on CIFAR-10, starting from Model C = 79.47%):

Technique Test Accuracy vs Model C
Model C (Residual CNN — baseline for comparison) 79.47% —
SE-ResNet (Channel Attention) 76.25% -3.22% ⚠️
Spatial Attention ResNet 81.06% +1.59% ✓
SE-ResNet + Label Smoothing + Cosine LR 83.12% +3.65% ✓

Honest observations:

  1. SE Attention did NOT help here. Adding the SE block actually hurt performance by ~3%. Possible reasons: the reduction ratio (16) may be too aggressive for this small model, BatchNorm interactions, or random initialization variance. A single run is not statistically conclusive. In literature, SE usually gives +0.5 to +1.5% — but it's not guaranteed.

  2. Spatial attention gave a small gain (+1.6%), suggesting that for CIFAR-10 (small 32×32 images), where-to-look matters slightly more than what-channels-to-focus-on.

  3. Label Smoothing + Cosine Decay was the biggest winner (+3.65%). These are "free lunch" techniques — no architecture changes, just better training recipe. This matches published results where good training schedules often beat exotic architectures.

  4. Optimizer study caveat: The Adam/SGD/AdamW comparison was run for only 10 epochs, so absolute accuracies are low (62-69%). The ranking (Adam > SGD > AdamW) is indicative, but all three would improve significantly with longer training.

  5. Grad-CAM visualization (on Model C): The heatmaps show the model correctly focuses on the main object in most cases (e.g., wings for airplanes, face for cats). When predictions are wrong, Grad-CAM often shows the model was looking at background or a co-occurring object.

  6. Filter visualization: First-layer filters in Model C show clear edge detectors, color-opposite patterns, and textures — classic CNN behavior matching what's seen in VGG/ResNet first layers.

  7. Confusion matrix (on best overall model, ResNet50 Fine-Tuned, 88%): The hardest classes are visually similar animal pairs — cat/dog and bird/deer. Vehicles (truck, automobile, ship) are easiest to classify. This reflects real visual similarity, not a model flaw.

Key lesson: Advanced techniques are not magic. Their benefit depends on the specific architecture, dataset, and training regime. Training recipe improvements (label smoothing, learning rate schedules) often beat architectural add-ons on small datasets like CIFAR-10.

Part 5: Written Analysis & Reflection (4 points)¶

A 400-word analysis covering performance comparison, interpretability findings, ethical considerations, fairness, and deployment recommendations — all grounded in the actual experimental results from Parts 1–4.

Written Analysis¶

1. Summary of Experiments: Custom vs Transfer Learning¶

Across eleven trained models, a clear pattern emerged. The best custom architecture (Model C, a ResNet-style CNN with ~700K parameters) reached 79.47% test accuracy, while the best transfer learning model (ResNet50 fine-tuned) reached 88.00% — an +8.5 percentage point gap. Even a frozen ResNet50 used only for feature extraction (85.32%) beat every custom model I designed. This aligns with the research consensus that on small datasets like CIFAR-10, features pretrained on large-scale ImageNet transfer extremely well. An interesting counterexample appeared with EfficientNetB0: fine-tuning (84.28%) performed worse than feature extraction (85.23%), likely because unfreezing BatchNorm layers disrupts the calibrated running statistics EfficientNet relies on. Among advanced techniques, label smoothing combined with cosine learning rate decay gave the biggest gain (+3.65% over Model C), while SE-attention unexpectedly hurt performance (-3%) in this single run — a reminder that architectural add-ons are not universally beneficial.

2. What the Models Learned (Interpretability)¶

Grad-CAM visualizations on Model C showed the network consistently attending to the main object: wings and fuselage for airplanes, faces and ears for cats, hulls for ships. When predictions were wrong, heatmaps often focused on background texture or a co-occurring object (e.g., grass for a misclassified dog), suggesting the model sometimes relied on contextual cues rather than the object itself. First-layer filter visualizations revealed classic edge detectors, color-opposition patterns, and simple textures — matching the hierarchical feature-learning narrative that dates back to HMAX and early CNN literature.

3. Ethical Concern: Dataset Bias¶

CIFAR-10 contains only 10 narrow categories of objects scraped from a specific era of the web. A classifier trained on it generalizes poorly to cultures, regions, or visual styles not represented in the training distribution. Deploying such a model for, say, wildlife monitoring in a region whose species are absent from ImageNet/CIFAR would produce confident but systematically wrong predictions. This bias is invisible from training metrics alone — the model does not know what it doesn't know.

4. Fairness Across Classes¶

The confusion matrix on ResNet50 fine-tuned shows a 21.4 percentage-point spread across classes: automobile (94.1%) vs cat (72.7%). Animals are systematically harder than vehicles. Data augmentation choices exacerbate this — horizontal flipping is safe for cars but could distort asymmetric animal poses. A fair system would require per-class augmentation policies and class-balanced loss weighting, neither of which is default.

5. Recommendations for Responsible Deployment¶

(1) Evaluate per-class metrics, not just overall accuracy. (2) Test on diverse, out-of-distribution samples before release. (3) Document training data provenance and known limitations. (4) Add calibrated confidence thresholds so the model can abstain on uncertain inputs. (5) Include human review for high-stakes decisions. Transfer learning's power cuts both ways: strong features also transfer strong biases.
